[context S07E19] gid=42581 Estelle: Joey! It’s Estelle! I just talked to the casting people; they loved you!
[context S07E19] gid=42582 Joey: They loved me! [to Monica and Phoebe]
[context S07E19] gid=42583 Estelle: Yeah, they wanna see you again tomorrow.
[context S07E19] gid=42584 Joey: Oh my God! [on phone]
[context S07E19] gid=42585 Estelle: There’s just one thing. Do you have a problem with full frontal nudity?
[context S07E19] gid=42586 Joey: Are you kidding me? I never rent a movie without it! Oh. Uh, okay uh let me call you back. [Listens; Listens; Hangs up.]
[context S07E19] gid=42587 Phoebe: What’s the matter?
[context S07E19] gid=42588 Joey: They want me to be totally naked in the movie!
[context S07E19] gid=42589 Monica: Wow!
[context S07E19] gid=42590 Joey: I know! My grandmother’s gonna see this!
[context S07E19] gid=42591 Phoebe: Grandma’s gonna have to get in line.
[context S07E19] description: Opening Credits
[context S07E19] description: Scene: Monica and Chandler’s, Monica is folding her laundry with Ross reading the paper and Phoebe standing in the kitchen.
[context S07E19] gid=42592 Phoebe: Hey the wedding is so close! Are you getting nervous?
[context S07E19] gid=42593 Monica: Yeah. But a part of me also can’t wait ‘til it’s over. Chandler and I have this pact not to have sex again until the wedding.
[context S07E19] gid=42594 Ross: A no sex pact huh? I actually have one of those going on with every woman in America.
[context S07E19] gid=42595 Monica: Hey Phoebe, will you give me a hand?
[context S07E19] gid=42596 Phoebe: Sure.
[context S07E19] gid=42597 Monica: I gotta make up the guest bedroom. Hey, Cousin Cassie is coming to stay with us a few days. [To Ross]
[context S07E19] gid=42598 Ross: Cassie?
[context S07E19] gid=42599 Monica: Uh-hmm.
[context S07E19] gid=42600 Ross: Wow, I haven’t seen her for like forever. I wonder if she still carries that Barbie everywhere she goes.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42601 Monica: Ross, she’s 25 years old.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42602 Ross: So what! I still have—No you’re probably right.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42603 Rachel: Hi! [entering]
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42604 Monica: Hey!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42605 Phoebe: Hey!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42606 Rachel: Hey Pheebs, can I talk to you over here for a second?
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42607 Phoebe: Yeah!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42608 Monica: Subtle guys!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42609 Phoebe: What?!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42610 Monica: I know you’re planning my surprise bridal shower.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42611 Rachel: Well okay—Well don’t ruin it! Just play along at least! [laughs]
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42612 Monica: Okay. Sorry. [She goes into the guest bedroom.]
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42613 Rachel: Oh my God! We have to throw her a shower?! [To Phoebe]
[context S07E19] description: Scene: Monica and Chandler's, Joey is entering.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42614 Monica: Hey! What did you decide to do about the movie?
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42615 Joey: I don’t know! It’s not like it’s porn! This is a serious, legitimate movie. Y’know? And the nudity is really important to the story.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42616 Monica: That’s what you say about porn.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42617 Joey: You’re right. Maybe I shouldn’t even go on the call back.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42618 Monica: No! No you should! A lot of major actors do nude scenes! I mean the chance to star in a movie? Come on!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42619 Joey: Well that’s true. And I am only naked in one scene. Plus it sounds really great. My character’s catholic and he falls in love with this Jewish girl. Who run away together and they get caught in this big rainstorm. So we go into this barn and undress each other and hold each other. It’s really sweet and-and tender.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42620 Monica: Plus, everyone’s gonna see your thing. [Giggles.]
[context S07E19] description: Scene: Phoebe's apartment, Phoebe and Rachel are trying to plan Monica’s shower.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42621 Phoebe: Well when can we have this shower?
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42622 Rachel: She has got so much going on we-we have only two options. We have Friday…
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42623 Phoebe: Well that’s only two days away. What is the other option?
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42624 Rachel: Yesterday!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42625 Phoebe: Well if we make it yesterday, woo-hoo! We’re done!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42626 Rachel: Oh my God Phoebe, this is impossible! We can’t do this by Friday! We have to find a place. We have to invite people! We have to get food! There’s just too much to do! It’s impossible! We can’t do it! We cannot do it! We cannot do it!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42627 Phoebe: Rachel, calm down!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42628 Rachel: Okay. I’m sorry. You’re right, you’re right. [calmly]
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42629 Phoebe: Just calm down woman! [grabs and shakes Rachel]
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42630 Rachel: Phoebe, I already, I already did.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42631 Phoebe: Oh okay. All right, then I need to calm down a little.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42632 Rachel: Okay. Okay. I think we can do this if we just get organized. All right? We have two days to plan this party. We just need to make fast decisions! Okay? All right, where are we gonna have it? [They sit down.]
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42633 Phoebe: Uh, here. What time?
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42634 Rachel: 4 o’clock. Food?
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42635 Phoebe: Finger sandwiches and tea.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42636 Rachel: Ooh great! Very Monica.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42637 Phoebe: And chili!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42638 Rachel: Ah you went one too far. Uh, flowers or balloons?
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42639 Phoebe: Both!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42640 Rachel: We’re paying for this y’know.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42641 Phoebe: Neither.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42642 Rachel: Okay. Umm, what should we do for the theme?
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42643 Phoebe: Lusts of the flesh.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42644 Rachel: What? [pause]
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42645 Phoebe: I don’t know. A cowboy theme? [Timidly]
[context S07E19] description: Scene: Monica and Chandler's, Monica is on the couch writing when Chandler enters to make his brief cameo.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42646 Chandler: Hey!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42647 Monica: Hey!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42648 Chandler: Y’know I’m-I’m really glad we decided not to sleep together before the wedding.
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42649 Monica: Oh boy me too!
[TARGET S07E19] gid=42650 Chandler: Y’know I was thinking if we had a…a big fight and uh we broke up for a few hours…

The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.

Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.

- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

You are a careful data curation assistant for a long-dialogue emotion-recognition benchmark built from the sitcom Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts.
Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.
Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.
Examine every TARGET utterance one by one before deciding which ones to select.
Output one review item for every TARGET utterance, with a selection label and a concise evidence-based reason.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.
Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.
Examine every TARGET utterance one by one before deciding which ones to select.
Output one review item for every TARGET utterance, with a selection label and a concise evidence-based reason.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

Return this JSON object shape:
{"batch_id": 29, "utterance_reviews": [{"global_utterance_id": 123, "season": 1, "episode": 1, "speaker": "Rachel", "is_selected": true, "reason": "no more than 5 sentences explaining the decision for this utterance"}]}

Allowed target global_utterance_id range: 42801..42850

Episode synopsis for every episode covered by this batch context:
S07E19: Ross’s and Monica's gorgeous cousin, Cassie (Denise Richards) visits, and Chandler, Ross, and Phoebe become attracted to her. Rachel and Phoebe throw a last-minute bridal shower for Monica. Joey auditions for a part which is perfect for him, apart from it calling for an uncircumcised actor (and Joey is circumcised). Upon finding out he lied about his 'downstairs' area, Monica tries to fix it so he can still get the part, using a variety of methods including Silly Putty and cold cuts.
S07E20: Rachel runs into Melissa (Winona Ryder), a former sorority sister with whom she once had a passionate kiss. However, Melissa denies it ever happened. Phoebe disbelieves that Rachel is capable of kissing a woman, so the latter recreates the kiss with surprising results: Melissa does remember and has feelings for Rachel. Meanwhile, Chandler is excited when he rents the same tuxedo that Pierce Brosnan had worn as James Bond, but feels outdone when Ross claims to have tried on the same tux that Val Kilmer had worn in Batman Forever. However, Ross’s tux turns out to be the one Val wore at a different movie.

Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.

Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.

Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

You are a careful data curation assistant for a long-dialogue emotion-recognition benchmark built from the sitcom Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts.
Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.
Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.
Examine every TARGET utterance one by one before deciding which ones to select.
Output one review item for every TARGET utterance, with a selection label and a concise evidence-based reason.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

Return this JSON object shape:
{"batch_id": 31, "utterance_reviews": [{"global_utterance_id": 123, "season": 1, "episode": 1, "speaker": "Rachel", "is_selected": true, "reason": "no more than 5 sentences explaining the decision for this utterance"}]}

The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.

Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

You are a careful data curation assistant for a long-dialogue emotion-recognition benchmark built from the sitcom Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts.
Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.
Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.
Examine every TARGET utterance one by one before deciding which ones to select.
Output one review item for every TARGET utterance, with a selection label and a concise evidence-based reason.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

You are a careful data curation assistant for a long-dialogue emotion-recognition benchmark built from the sitcom Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts.
Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.
Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.
Examine every TARGET utterance one by one before deciding which ones to select.
Output one review item for every TARGET utterance, with a selection label and a concise evidence-based reason.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

You are a careful data curation assistant for a long-dialogue emotion-recognition benchmark built from the sitcom Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts.
Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.
Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.
Examine every TARGET utterance one by one before deciding which ones to select.
Output one review item for every TARGET utterance, with a selection label and a concise evidence-based reason.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

Return this JSON object shape:
{"batch_id": 35, "utterance_reviews": [{"global_utterance_id": 123, "season": 1, "episode": 1, "speaker": "Rachel", "is_selected": true, "reason": "no more than 5 sentences explaining the decision for this utterance"}]}

Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.
Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

[context S07E21] description: Flashback to Joey interrupting a bath Monica and Chandler are sharing in The One With All The Kissing. Monica dives underwater as Joey opens the door.

[context S07E21] description: Joey leaves and Monica comes up for air.

[context S07E21] description: Cut back to Central Perk.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.

A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

You are a careful data curation assistant for a long-dialogue emotion-recognition benchmark built from the sitcom Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts.
Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.
Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.
Examine every TARGET utterance one by one before deciding which ones to select.
Output one review item for every TARGET utterance, with a selection label and a concise evidence-based reason.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

You are a careful data curation assistant for a long-dialogue emotion-recognition benchmark built from the sitcom Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts.
Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.
Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.
Examine every TARGET utterance one by one before deciding which ones to select.
Output one review item for every TARGET utterance, with a selection label and a concise evidence-based reason.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

You are a careful data curation assistant for a long-dialogue emotion-recognition benchmark built from the sitcom Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts.
Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.
Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.
Examine every TARGET utterance one by one before deciding which ones to select.
Output one review item for every TARGET utterance, with a selection label and a concise evidence-based reason.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

Episode synopsis for every episode covered by this batch context:
S07E22: Chandler tries to reconcile with his estranged gay father (Kathleen Turner), at the behest of Monica: the couple goes to Vegas to attend one of Mr. Bing's drag shows, where the father and son finally reconcile, and Mr. Bing agrees to attend the wedding. Rachel, who is an irresponsible driver, takes Monica's Porsche for a spin with a fearful Ross, and ends up getting caught driving without a valid license. She then flirts with the officer to avoid getting a ticket. Later, Ross is pulled over for driving too slowly on the freeway and attempts to flirt his way out of getting a ticket as well, but to no avail. Meanwhile, Joey takes Phoebe's advice about his masculinity, which results in him trying on women's underwear.
S07E23: Joey gets an important role in a major movie about World War I, learns the art of enunciation (and therein spitting) from his famous co-star (Gary Oldman), and later discovers that he is supposed to work on the day of Monica’s and Chandler's wedding. Chandler's fear of commitment overwhelms him and he runs away before the wedding. Phoebe finds a positive pregnancy test in Monica's bathroom trash, and assumes it is Monica’s. Joey is relieved that he only has to shoot one scene before he can leave to officiate the wedding, but his co-star turns up drunk and ruins his chances of making it to the wedding on time. Chandler is eventually found hiding in his office, but disappears again upon overhearing Phoebe and Rachel discussing Monica's assumed pregnancy. Luckily, he turns up again and starts accepting that he is going to be a father. Joey arrives just in time to perform the ceremony while still wearing his World War I movie costume. Chandler and Monica finally become husband and wife while marrying to the tune of the song "Everlong" by Foo Fighters. At the end of the episode, Chandler announces to Monica that he knows about the baby. Monica is surprised and denies the fact that she is pregnant which brings up the question about who is. The camera then zooms into Rachel's face suggesting that the pregnancy test is hers.

messages.content:
You are a careful data curation assistant for a long-dialogue emotion-recognition benchmark built from the sitcom Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts.
Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.
Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.
Examine every TARGET utterance one by one before deciding which ones to select.
Output one review item for every TARGET utterance, with a selection label and a concise evidence-based reason.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

Return this JSON object shape:
{"batch_id": 46, "utterance_reviews": [{"global_utterance_id": 123, "season": 1, "episode": 1, "speaker": "Rachel", "is_selected": true, "reason": "no more than 5 sentences explaining the decision for this utterance"}]}

Episode synopsis for every episode covered by this batch context:
S07E23: Joey gets an important role in a major movie about World War I, learns the art of enunciation (and therein spitting) from his famous co-star (Gary Oldman), and later discovers that he is supposed to work on the day of Monica’s and Chandler's wedding. Chandler's fear of commitment overwhelms him and he runs away before the wedding. Phoebe finds a positive pregnancy test in Monica's bathroom trash, and assumes it is Monica’s. Joey is relieved that he only has to shoot one scene before he can leave to officiate the wedding, but his co-star turns up drunk and ruins his chances of making it to the wedding on time. Chandler is eventually found hiding in his office, but disappears again upon overhearing Phoebe and Rachel discussing Monica's assumed pregnancy. Luckily, he turns up again and starts accepting that he is going to be a father. Joey arrives just in time to perform the ceremony while still wearing his World War I movie costume. Chandler and Monica finally become husband and wife while marrying to the tune of the song "Everlong" by Foo Fighters. At the end of the episode, Chandler announces to Monica that he knows about the baby. Monica is surprised and denies the fact that she is pregnant which brings up the question about who is. The camera then zooms into Rachel's face suggesting that the pregnancy test is hers.

You are a careful data curation assistant for a long-dialogue emotion-recognition benchmark built from the sitcom Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts.
Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.
Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.
Examine every TARGET utterance one by one before deciding which ones to select.
Output one review item for every TARGET utterance, with a selection label and a concise evidence-based reason.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

{"batch_id": 47, "utterance_reviews": [{"global_utterance_id": 123, "season": 1, "episode": 1, "speaker": "Rachel", "is_selected": true, "reason": "no more than 5 sentences explaining the decision for this utterance"}]}

S07E23: Joey gets an important role in a major movie about World War I, learns the art of enunciation (and therein spitting) from his famous co-star (Gary Oldman), and later discovers that he is supposed to work on the day of Monica’s and Chandler's wedding. Chandler's fear of commitment overwhelms him and he runs away before the wedding. Phoebe finds a positive pregnancy test in Monica's bathroom trash, and assumes it is Monica’s. Joey is relieved that he only has to shoot one scene before he can leave to officiate the wedding, but his co-star turns up drunk and ruins his chances of making it to the wedding on time. Chandler is eventually found hiding in his office, but disappears again upon overhearing Phoebe and Rachel discussing Monica's assumed pregnancy. Luckily, he turns up again and starts accepting that he is going to be a father. Joey arrives just in time to perform the ceremony while still wearing his World War I movie costume. Chandler and Monica finally become husband and wife while marrying to the tune of the song "Everlong" by Foo Fighters. At the end of the episode, Chandler announces to Monica that he knows about the baby. Monica is surprised and denies the fact that she is pregnant which brings up the question about who is. The camera then zooms into Rachel's face suggesting that the pregnancy test is hers.

You are a careful data curation assistant for a long-dialogue emotion-recognition benchmark built from the sitcom Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts.
Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.
Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.
Examine every TARGET utterance one by one before deciding which ones to select.
Output one review item for every TARGET utterance, with a selection label and a concise evidence-based reason.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

Return this JSON object shape:
{"batch_id": 48, "utterance_reviews": [{"global_utterance_id": 123, "season": 1, "episode": 1, "speaker": "Rachel", "is_selected": true, "reason": "no more than 5 sentences explaining the decision for this utterance"}]}

Episode synopsis for every episode covered by this batch context:
S07E23: Joey gets an important role in a major movie about World War I, learns the art of enunciation (and therein spitting) from his famous co-star (Gary Oldman), and later discovers that he is supposed to work on the day of Monica’s and Chandler's wedding. Chandler's fear of commitment overwhelms him and he runs away before the wedding. Phoebe finds a positive pregnancy test in Monica's bathroom trash, and assumes it is Monica’s. Joey is relieved that he only has to shoot one scene before he can leave to officiate the wedding, but his co-star turns up drunk and ruins his chances of making it to the wedding on time. Chandler is eventually found hiding in his office, but disappears again upon overhearing Phoebe and Rachel discussing Monica's assumed pregnancy. Luckily, he turns up again and starts accepting that he is going to be a father. Joey arrives just in time to perform the ceremony while still wearing his World War I movie costume. Chandler and Monica finally become husband and wife while marrying to the tune of the song "Everlong" by Foo Fighters. At the end of the episode, Chandler announces to Monica that he knows about the baby. Monica is surprised and denies the fact that she is pregnant which brings up the question about who is. The camera then zooms into Rachel's face suggesting that the pregnancy test is hers.

You are a careful data curation assistant for a long-dialogue emotion-recognition benchmark built from the sitcom Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts.
Return only valid JSON. Do not include Markdown, comments, or extra text.
Your goal is high-recall candidate discovery: find target utterances whose true speaker emotion may require long-range dialogue history.
Treat utterance lines as character dialogue and description lines as screenplay stage directions, including scene changes, facial expressions, actions, entrances, and exits.
Examine every TARGET utterance one by one before deciding which ones to select.
Output one review item for every TARGET utterance, with a selection label and a concise evidence-based reason.

Task:
The input is from Friends (老友记) screenplay transcripts. Utterance lines are character dialogue; description lines are stage directions that may include setting, actions, expressions, entrances, and exits.
For every TARGET utterance, decide whether it is a strong candidate for requiring long-range historical context to identify the speaker's true emotion correctly.
Context lines are included only to stabilize local reading. Do not select context-only utterances.
Inspect the TARGET utterances one by one in order. Do not only pick the most dramatic or most famous lines.

Definition of long-range dependency:
A target utterance is a candidate only if its emotional interpretation likely depends on information beyond the immediate line or very short local exchange, such as earlier scenes, earlier episodes, relationship history, recurring character patterns, or unresolved past events.

Four useful long-range dependency types:
1. relationship_history: emotion depends on relationship history, past romance/conflict/family dynamics, breakups, betrayals, promises, jealousy, or role expectations.
2. character_trait_or_habit: emotion depends on stable character traits or recurring habits, such as sarcasm, defensiveness, control needs, avoidance, insecurity, or unusual expression style.
3. past_event_reference: the line weakly refers to older events through terms such as again, that thing, after what happened, you know why, or another indirect allusion.
4. surface_true_emotion_mismatch: surface wording differs from the speaker's likely true emotion because of sarcasm, pretending, suppression, face-saving, awkwardness, or joking to hide distress.

Common AI mistakes to avoid:
1. Do not confuse current-scene context with long-range dependency. If the emotion is clear from the current scene or nearby lines, do not select it.
2. Do not overinterpret ordinary jokes, factual replies, or functional transitions as deep emotion. If historical evidence would be decorative rather than necessary, skip it.

Selection policy:
- Mark at most 20 TARGET utterances as is_selected=true.
- Prefer recall over precision, but every selected item must have a concrete short-context failure mode.
- Do not use future lines after the target utterance as evidence.
- Return one review item for every TARGET utterance, even when is_selected=false.
- For each review item, write reason in no more than 5 sentences.
- If is_selected=true, the reason must explain both the likely long-range dependency and why short context may fail.
- If is_selected=false, the reason should briefly say why local context is enough or why the line is not a good long-context candidate.

Return this JSON object shape:
{"batch_id": 49, "utterance_reviews": [{"global_utterance_id": 123, "season": 1, "episode": 1, "speaker": "Rachel", "is_selected": true, "reason": "no more than 5 sentences explaining the decision for this utterance"}]}
